title: A school of the Lord's service (Rule, Prologue)
word: A school of the Lord's service
hookLine: nothing harsh, nothing burdensome: a school for beginners
tomorrow: a long list of tools. which one does Benedict save for last?

cards: A new job hands you a handbook, and it opens with what gets you fired. A gym contract opens with the cancellation fee. So here's an odd one.

A rulebook for monks, people who hand their whole day over to a shared life of prayer and work, opens with a single word: listen. Not a rule. A father's voice: listen, my son, and incline the ear of your heart.
And near the end of that opening, the Prologue, it makes a promise no handbook makes. Nothing harsh. Nothing burdensome.
From a monastery? How does that add up?

teach.b: The answer is one word. We are about to set up, Benedict says, a school of the Lord's service. A school.
Not a fortress, not a club for people who are already holy. A place for learning, where not knowing yet is the normal state of things. That's why harshness isn't the goal.
He's honest that it won't all be easy.

If something feels a little strict, to correct faults or to protect love, don't be frightened and run from the way, he says; the way in is bound to be narrow at the start. Then he saves his best line for last.
As you go further in, your heart grows wide, and you run the way of God's commandments with a sweetness of love too deep for words. He's echoing a psalm.
In the King James: "I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart." Narrow at the door, wide inside.

And here's the detail to tell a friend: on the last page of the same book, Benedict calls the whole thing a little rule written for beginners. The rulebook calls itself a beginner's book. So the puzzle solves itself.
A school expects mistakes and plans for them. Nobody arrives finished. You show up, and begin, and begin again.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Benedict, and some communities read a portion of it aloud each day; some Christians outside monasteries, often called oblates, also shape their lives by it.

games.q: what does “a school of the lord's service” mean?
o: a church school where monks taught village children
a training camp with hard drills for new monks
Benedict's picture of the monastery as a place to learn

s: a monastery rule is mostly a list of harsh demands
the popular picture. Benedict hopes to lay down nothing harsh, nothing burdensome.
Benedict's Rule opens with the word listen

games.q: your friend wants to start running, but she quits every time she can't finish a full mile. what would Benedict's school say?
o: wait until she's fit enough to do it properly.
start with one easy block, and expect to start over.
push through the pain; narrow means it should hurt.
games.why: Benedict wrote a little rule for beginners: narrow at the start, and nobody expected to arrive finished. beginning again is the school.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write one thing you started and let drop: a habit, a prayer, a promise. Under it, write the smallest way to start again, small enough to feel almost silly.
Then sit with the page in your hands, a beginner's page.

wordCard.voice: A school of the Lord's service. Benedict's picture of a shared life of faith: a place to learn, with nothing harsh and nothing burdensome.

orig.note: Latin: listen. the first word of the Rule of Benedict: ausculta, o fili, listen, my son.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: a school for beginners, narrow at the door and wide inside. Day sixteen-twenty-six, done.
